verifyNote: Written from standard UK low vision practice and guidance from the College of Optometrists, RNIB and the Department of Health certification guidance. Certification criteria, forms and benefits differ between England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland and change over time: check the current version for your nation.

topics.title: Causes and impact of visual impairment in the UK
topics.summary: Low vision means sight loss that can't be fully corrected with glasses, contact lenses, medicine or surgery and that affects everyday life. In older adults it's mainly caused by age-related macular degeneration, glaucoma, diabetic eye disease and cataract; in children, cerebral visual impairment is now the most common cause. The impact goes far beyond reading: falls, isolation, depression and loss of independence are common.
keyPoints: More than 2 million people in the UK live with sight loss that affects their daily lives (RNIB estimate), and numbers are rising as the population ages.
Leading causes in older adults: AMD, glaucoma, cataract, diabetic retinopathy and uncorrected refractive error.
In children in the UK, cerebral (cortical) visual impairment is the most common cause of visual impairment.
Central field loss (for example AMD) mainly affects reading, faces and fine detail; peripheral field loss (for example advanced glaucoma, retinitis pigmentosa) mainly affects mobility.
Sight loss is linked to falls, depression, social isolation and loss of employment.
Charles Bonnet syndrome (vivid visual hallucinations with insight) is common in people with sight loss and is often not reported because people fear it means mental illness.
examTraps: Thinking low vision only affects reading: mobility, faces, TV, cooking and wellbeing matter too.
Forgetting to ask about Charles Bonnet syndrome: a simple explanation can be a huge relief.
Assuming one type of aid suits everyone with the same acuity.

diagram.description: Three simulated views of a street scene: normal vision; central field loss (a dark blurred patch in the centre, as in AMD); peripheral field loss (only a small central tunnel visible, as in advanced glaucoma or retinitis pigmentosa). Label the main daily tasks affected under each.
labels: Peripheral loss (e.g. RP, glaucoma): mobility, trips

goDeeper.heading: Charles Bonnet syndrome
goDeeper.body: When the brain gets less visual input, it can produce its own images: patterns, people, animals or scenes, sometimes very detailed. People know they aren't real. It's not a mental health problem, often settles over time, and is common in AMD. Ask about it gently in every low vision assessment, reassure, and signpost to support such as the Esme's Umbrella campaign or RNIB.

goDeeper.heading: Emotional impact
goDeeper.body: Losing sight is often described like a bereavement. Depression rates are high in people with sight loss. Listen, acknowledge feelings, and signpost to emotional support (for example RNIB's helpline and counselling, local sight loss charities, the Eye Clinic Liaison Officer). Practical solutions help but don't replace being heard.

goDeeper.heading: Falls and safety
goDeeper.body: Reduced acuity, contrast sensitivity and fields all increase the risk of falls. Multifocal glasses can make steps harder to judge. Practical advice includes good lighting on stairs, contrasting edges on steps, removing trip hazards, and considering single-vision distance glasses for walking outdoors.

topics.title: Low vision assessment
topics.summary: A low vision assessment finds out what the person wants to do and what their vision allows, then matches help to their goals. It includes a detailed history, acuity at an appropriate distance, near acuity and reading speed, contrast sensitivity and a look at central fields and eccentric viewing.
keyPoints: Start with goals: what would they most like to do (read post, watch TV, recognise faces, cook, get around)?
Measure distance acuity with a logMAR chart at a closer distance (for example 2 m or 1 m) so they read more letters; adjust the score for distance.
Measure near acuity with continuous text in N-point print sizes and note reading speed; newspaper print is about N8–N10.
Contrast sensitivity predicts real-world difficulty better than acuity alone.
Check central fields (for example Amsler or a scotoma map) and whether they use eccentric viewing (a preferred retinal locus).
Refraction still matters: a careful refraction with larger steps (for example ±1.00 D) can improve vision.
examTraps: Testing distance acuity only at 6 m: few letters are read, so small changes are missed.
Measuring near acuity only with single words instead of continuous text.

diagram.description: A flow chart: History and goals → Distance VA (logMAR at 2 m/1 m) → Refraction (larger steps) → Near VA and reading speed → Contrast sensitivity → Central field and eccentric viewing → Trial of aids → Plan, training and referral.

goDeeper.heading: Adjusting acuity for distance
goDeeper.body: LogMAR at a shorter distance: add log₁₀(standard distance ÷ test distance). A chart designed for 4 m read at 1 m: add log₁₀(4) = 0.60. If the patient reads to 0.80 at 1 m, their 4 m equivalent is 1.40. Recording as, for example, '0.80 at 1 m' is also fine as long as the distance is clear.

goDeeper.heading: Eccentric viewing
goDeeper.body: With a central scotoma, people learn to use a healthier area of retina next to it, the preferred retinal locus. Many do this naturally; others benefit from training to place the scotoma consistently, often above or to one side of the target. Asking the patient to look at your nose and describe what they can see of your face helps locate the scotoma.

goDeeper.heading: Reading performance
goDeeper.body: Reading speed charts (for example MNREAD-style continuous text) give the threshold print size, the critical print size (the smallest print read at full speed) and the maximum reading speed. Aids are set to give print comfortably larger than the critical print size, because reading at threshold is slow and tiring.

checklist.title: Low vision assessment outline
steps: Ask about the person's main goals, daily tasks, current aids, lighting, falls, mood and Charles Bonnet symptoms.
Measure distance acuity with a logMAR chart at an appropriate shorter distance and record the distance.
Refract with larger steps where needed and check whether vision improves.
Measure near acuity with continuous text (N-point) and note reading speed and critical print size.
Assess central fields (Amsler or scotoma mapping) and eccentric viewing.
Calculate magnification needed for the main goal and try suitable aids with good lighting.
Agree a plan, demonstrate the aid, give written instructions and arrange follow-up or referral (rehabilitation, ECLO, charities).

topics.title: Magnification: types and how much is needed
topics.summary: Magnification makes the image on the retina bigger so it lands on more working cells. There are four ways to do it: make the object bigger, bring it closer, use an optical device that enlarges the angle (such as a telescope), or project it electronically. Working out how much is needed starts from the patient's current near acuity and the size of print they want to read.
keyPoints: Relative size magnification: make the object bigger (large print, bigger phone text).
Relative distance magnification: bring the object closer (halving the distance doubles the retinal image).
Angular magnification: optical devices such as telescopes enlarge the angle the object subtends.
Electronic (projection) magnification: video magnifiers, tablets and apps.
Magnification needed ≈ current print size read ÷ target print size, then add a reserve for fluent reading. For example reads N24, wants N8 → 3× (more for comfort).
Equivalent power for near (with a 25 cm reference): F ≈ 4 × M dioptres, so 3× ≈ +12 D.
examTraps: Forgetting the reading reserve and prescribing just enough to reach threshold.
Ignoring that more magnification means a smaller field of view and shorter working distance.
Mixing up the reference distances used by different manufacturers (25 cm vs other conventions).

diagram.description: Four panels showing an eye looking at a letter: (1) larger letter at the same distance (relative size), (2) same letter brought closer (relative distance), (3) a telescope enlarging the angle (angular), (4) a screen showing an enlarged letter (electronic). Show the bigger retinal image in each.

goDeeper.heading: A worked example
goDeeper.body: A patient reads N20 with their reading glasses at 25 cm and wants to read N5 bank statements. Magnification needed = 20 ÷ 5 = 4×. Add a comfort reserve (for example aim for 1.5–2× their critical print size), giving roughly 5–6×. Equivalent power ≈ 4 × 5 = +20 D (or 24 D for 6×). Then try devices of that strength and adjust to what works in practice.

goDeeper.heading: Field of view and working distance
goDeeper.body: As magnification goes up, the field of view through a lens gets smaller and the working distance gets shorter (for a spectacle magnifier, about 100 / F cm). People reading with a +20 D add must hold text about 5 cm away. Hand magnifiers give a larger field when held close to the eye. Matching the device to the task (spot reading versus long reading) matters as much as the number.

goDeeper.heading: Why electronic aids are so useful
goDeeper.body: Video magnifiers and tablets offer high magnification with a comfortable working distance, adjustable contrast and colour reversal (light text on dark), and can read text aloud. They are often the best option for longer reading at high magnifications, although some people find them harder to use, and they need power and some training.

topics.title: Magnifiers, telescopes and electronic aids
topics.summary: Each type of low vision aid suits different tasks and people. Hand magnifiers are portable and flexible; stand magnifiers suit people with tremor or long reading; spectacle magnifiers keep hands free; telescopes help at distance; and electronic aids offer the most magnification and contrast control. Good demonstration and training are what make an aid actually get used.
keyPoints: Hand magnifiers: cheap and portable, good for short tasks (labels, prices); need a steady hand and correct distance.
Stand magnifiers: rest on the page at a fixed distance, good with tremor and for longer reading; they form an image at a finite distance, so the patient usually needs their reading glasses or an add.
Spectacle magnifiers (high reading adds): hands free and wide field, but very short working distance; base-in prisms help binocular use up to about +10 D.

Telescopes: Galilean (simple, upright image, low power) and Keplerian (sharper, more powerful, need prisms to correct the image). They narrow the field and are mainly for spotting tasks like reading signs or watching TV.
Electronic aids: desktop video magnifiers, portable devices, tablets and smartphone apps with zoom, contrast reversal and text-to-speech.
Many patients abandon aids that weren't demonstrated well; give training, written instructions and follow-up.
examTraps: Forgetting that stand magnifier users usually need their reading correction.
Recommending a telescope for walking around: the field is too narrow.
Choosing the strongest aid instead of the one that fits the task and the person.

diagram.description: Side-by-side sketches of: a hand magnifier held close to the eye, an illuminated stand magnifier resting on a page with the eye using reading glasses, high-add spectacles with text held close, a small spectacle-mounted telescope for distance, and a desktop video magnifier.

goDeeper.heading: Getting the most from a hand magnifier
goDeeper.body: Hold the magnifier at its focal distance from the page (for a +12 D lens about 8 cm). If the patient wears distance glasses and holds the page at exactly the focal length, light leaves the lens parallel and the eye-to-lens distance only changes the field of view: closer to the eye gives a wider view. Many illuminated magnifiers include an LED light, which helps a lot.

goDeeper.heading: Telescopes
goDeeper.body: A Galilean telescope (positive objective, negative eyepiece) gives an upright image, is short and light, but usually limited to about 4×. A Keplerian telescope (two positive lenses) is longer, needs prisms to make the image upright, but gives better optics and higher power. Magnification M = −Feyepiece / Fobjective. Telescopes can be focused for near with a reading cap.

goDeeper.heading: Technology and apps
goDeeper.body: Smartphones and tablets now do much of what dedicated devices did: magnification, high-contrast modes, text-to-speech, apps that read text or describe scenes, and accessibility settings built into the operating system. Show patients these settings on their own devices, and signpost to digital skills support from sight loss charities.

cases.scenario: A 72-year-old with geographic atrophy (logMAR 1.0 each eye) wants to watch football on TV and read cooking instructions on packets.
cases.question: Which aids might help each task?
cases.modelAnswer: TV: sit closer (relative distance magnification), consider a spectacle-mounted or hand-held telescope set for the viewing distance, or a larger screen. Packets: a hand or illuminated stand magnifier for short spot reading, or a smartphone camera with zoom/text-to-speech. Add good task lighting and train the patient with each device.

topics.askClaude: Give me five daily tasks a low vision patient struggles with and ask which aid I'd suggest for each and why.

topics.title: Lighting, contrast and non-optical aids
topics.summary: Simple changes often help as much as magnification. Good, well-placed lighting, higher contrast, reducing glare, and using touch or sound instead of sight can make everyday tasks possible again. These are cheap, quick to try and easy to forget.
keyPoints: Task lighting: a bright, adjustable lamp placed close to the task and to the side of the better eye, avoiding shadows and reflections.
Older eyes often need around three times more light than younger eyes for the same task.
Increase contrast: bold-lined paper, thick black pens, a typoscope (a black card with a slot for reading lines), contrasting chopping boards and tape on step edges.
Glare control: hats with brims, side shields and tinted filters (often yellow or amber for glare and contrast, especially in cataract or retinitis pigmentosa).
Sensory substitution: audiobooks, talking clocks, screen readers, bump-on dots for appliances and liquid level indicators.
Mobility: symbol canes signal sight loss; long canes and guide dogs need training from rehabilitation services.
examTraps: Focusing only on optical aids and forgetting lighting.
Assuming tints always help: always let the patient try them in real conditions.
Forgetting that rehabilitation services (not optometrists) provide mobility training.

diagram.description: A person reading at a table with an adjustable lamp placed low and to the side of their better eye, light falling on the page without reflecting into their eyes. Next to it, a typoscope (black card with a rectangular slot) over a page of text.

goDeeper.heading: Lighting advice
goDeeper.body: Bring the light to the task rather than lighting the whole room more. Position it to avoid shadows from the head or hands, and so it doesn't reflect off glossy paper into the eyes. Daylight-type LED lamps are cool and efficient. Even, bright lighting on stairs and in kitchens helps safety. Let people try different light levels: some (for example with corneal problems or cone dystrophies) prefer less.

goDeeper.heading: Contrast at home
goDeeper.body: Use contrasting colours: a dark mug for milky drinks, white plates on a dark tablecloth, coloured tape on light switches and the edge of each step. Reduce clutter and patterns that hide objects. Bold-line writing paper and black felt-tip pens make writing easier to read back.

goDeeper.heading: Filters and glare
goDeeper.body: Glare from cataract, corneal scarring or retinal disease can be disabling. Wrap-around sunglasses, side shields and peaked caps block stray light. Coloured filters (yellow, amber, orange) cut short-wavelength light and can improve comfort and apparent contrast. Patients should try filters outdoors and indoors before buying, as preferences vary a lot.

topics.title: Certification, registration and support services
topics.summary: In England, a consultant ophthalmologist can certify someone as sight impaired or severely sight impaired using the Certificate of Vision Impairment (CVI). The certificate goes to the local council, which offers registration and a rehabilitation assessment. Optometrists play a key role in spotting who might be eligible, explaining the process and signposting to support long before and after certification.
keyPoints: Two categories: sight impaired (partially sighted) and severely sight impaired (blind).
The CVI is completed by a consultant ophthalmologist; it records acuity, fields and diagnosis.
Registration with the local council is voluntary and opens up rehabilitation, equipment and some benefits and concessions.
People who aren't yet eligible can still get help: Referral of Vision Impairment and Letter of Vision Impairment forms let optometrists and others refer people to social services directly.
Eye Clinic Liaison Officers (ECLOs) in hospital clinics give practical and emotional support around diagnosis.
Different forms and processes apply in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
examTraps: Saying optometrists certify sight impairment: consultant ophthalmologists do.
Waiting for certification before referring for help: rehabilitation can start earlier.
Forgetting to tell patients about the DVLA if their vision or fields fall below the standard.

diagram.description: A flow chart: Optometrist or clinic identifies sight loss → (if eligible) consultant ophthalmologist completes CVI → copy to GP, patient and local council → council offers registration and needs assessment → rehabilitation, equipment, benefits. A side branch from the optometrist directly to social services via Referral/Letter of Vision Impairment for people not yet certified.
labels: Referral or Letter of Vision Impairment

goDeeper.heading: Certification criteria (outline)
goDeeper.body: Severely sight impaired includes, for example, acuity worse than 3/60 with a full field; 3/60 to worse than 6/60 with a very contracted field; or 6/60 or better with a very contracted field, especially if the lower field is lost. Sight impaired includes, for example, 3/60 to 6/60 with a full field; up to 6/24 with moderate field contraction; or 6/18 or better with a gross field defect. Use the current official guidance for exact criteria.

goDeeper.heading: What registration can offer
goDeeper.body: A rehabilitation (habilitation) assessment for daily living and mobility skills, equipment, and help at home. Concessions may include a Blind Person's Allowance (tax), a reduced TV licence for severely sight impaired people, a Blue Badge for severely sight impaired people, travel concessions and a Disabled Persons Railcard. Benefits such as Personal Independence Payment depend on how sight loss affects the person, not on registration alone.

goDeeper.heading: The optometrist's role
goDeeper.body: Notice when vision is reducing, explain what certification is and ask whether the patient would like it, refer to the hospital eye service if needed, provide low vision care, and refer directly to social services and charities for support. Discuss driving and the DVLA, work and education support (for example Access to Work), and emotional support, and record what you discussed.

cases.scenario: A 45-year-old teacher with retinitis pigmentosa has acuities of 6/9 but fields constricted to about 10° in each eye. She is still driving.
cases.question: What do you need to discuss and do?
cases.modelAnswer: Her fields are very likely below the DVLA standard: explain she must tell the DVLA and stop driving until they decide, and record the advice. She may meet criteria for certification (good acuity but a very contracted field); refer to the hospital eye service to discuss this. Signpost Access to Work for support in her job, mobility training through social services, and RP support groups (for example Retina UK).

topics.askClaude: Explain the difference between certification and registration, then give me two patients and ask whether they might be eligible and what support I'd signpost.
